title: Top of the class, then a slump?
hook: The best scorers do worse next time. Did they get lazy, or is something else going on?

knows: that test results involve some luck
doesNotKnow: score = skill + luck as a model

misconception: If top scorers do worse next time, something about them changed: complacency, a jinx, or a coach's praise.
objective: The learner can explain that extreme scores tend to include extra luck, which is not repeated, so a group selected for extreme results moves back toward the average on a retest with no change in skill.

claims.text: If a score is skill plus luck with equal spread, and the luck is drawn fresh each test, the correlation between two tests is 0.5 and a group's expected test-2 score sits halfway between its test-1 average and the overall average.
claims.source: X1 = S + L1, X2 = S + L2 with S, L1, L2 independent, equal variance v: cov(X1, X2) = v, var(Xi) = 2v, so r = 0.5. For jointly normal scores E[X2 | X1] = mean + 0.5 (X1 - mean); averaging over any group selected on X1 gives the halfway rule.

claims.text: In the simulated class of 1,000, the top 10% on test 1 averaged about 76 and then about 62 on test 2, with an overall average near 50.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/praise-then-slump/model.ts, seed 1886: score = 50 + 15 (skill + luck)/sqrt(2), rounded and clipped to 0-100. Re-run: class means 49.6 and 49.5, r = 0.48; top 10% 76.1 -> 62.4; top 1% 88.9 -> 71.9; bottom 10% 23.7 -> 37.6.

claims.text: The bottom scorers on test 1 score higher on average on test 2, for the same reason.
claims.source: Same model and seed: bottom 10% 23.7 -> 37.6; bottom 50% 37.4 -> 43.6. Follows from the halfway rule in c1.

claims.text: Francis Galton named the effect 'regression' in 1886, from the heights of parents and their adult children.
claims.source: F. Galton (1886), 'Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature', Journal of the Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland 15: 246-263.

recall.question: A coach shouts at the players who had their worst game ever. Next game, most of them play better. What does that show about shouting?
options: Not much: after a worst-ever game, better is likely anyway
recall.why: A worst-ever game usually includes bad luck, which does not repeat. Players picked for an extreme result drift back toward their average whatever the coach does.
